prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

When daylighting into a building interior, this daylighting structure attenuates the brightness of a setting sun or a winter-time incoming light of small elevation angles, and causes the incoming light to be diffusely emitted toward the ceiling surface or into a deep portion of the indoor space domain regardless of the elevation angle thereof. An incoming light (E20) of 20° in elevation angle is caused to be diffusely emitted toward the ceiling surface on the internal upper side of the building through the refraction and reflection actions mediated by a light-transmitting material mounted in a horizontal direction opening of a wall. The light-transmitting material comprises: an outdoor region curved surface wherethrough the incoming light is refracted and let into the interior of the light-transmitting material in a focused form; a lower side reflection surface internally reflecting the refracted incoming light; and an indoor region curved surface wherefrom the internally reflected light is refracted and emitted toward the ceiling surface in a diffused form. Also disclosed are the installation wherein the light-transmitting material is inclined from the illustrated horizontal state, and the installation of a plurality of the light-transmitting materials, each in upper and lower directions and left and right directions.

outputs.L1: When introducing daylight into a building interior, this daylighting structure reduces the brightness of light from the setting sun or winter sunlight entering at low elevation angles and diffusely directs the incoming light toward the ceiling surface or deep into the interior space, regardless of its elevation angle. Incoming light (E20) at an elevation angle of 20° is diffusely emitted toward the upper interior ceiling surface of the building through refraction and reflection by a light-transmitting material installed horizontally within an opening in a wall. The light-transmitting material comprises: an outdoor-side curved surface through which the incoming light is refracted and introduced into the material in a focused form; a lower reflective surface that internally reflects the refracted incoming light; and an indoor-side curved surface through which the internally reflected light is refracted and emitted toward the ceiling surface in a diffused form. Also disclosed are an installation in which the light-transmitting material is inclined relative to the illustrated horizontal position, and an installation comprising a plurality of light-transmitting materials arranged vertically and horizontally.
outputs.L2: This daylighting system reduces the glare of low-angle sunlight, such as light from the setting sun or winter sun, while directing it diffusely toward the ceiling or farther into the building interior, irrespective of its elevation angle. Light entering at an elevation angle of 20° (E20) passes through a light-transmitting member installed horizontally in an opening in the wall. Through refraction and reflection within the member, the light is diffusely projected onto the upper interior ceiling surface. The light-transmitting member includes an exterior-side curved surface that refracts and focuses the incident light into the member, a lower reflective surface that internally reflects the refracted light, and an interior-side curved surface that refracts the reflected light again and disperses it toward the ceiling. Additional configurations include mounting the light-transmitting member at an incline rather than in the illustrated horizontal orientation, as well as arranging multiple members vertically and horizontally.
outputs.L3:
The daylighting structure is designed to reduce the brightness and glare of low-elevation sunlight, such as light from the setting sun or winter sun. Regardless of the incoming light’s elevation angle, the structure redirects daylight toward the ceiling or deeper into the indoor space, helping to create more even and comfortable illumination.

For example, when sunlight enters at an elevation angle of 20°, it is refracted as it passes through the structure, reflected internally, and then emitted diffusely toward the interior ceiling. This controlled optical path limits direct glare while allowing natural light to reach farther into the room.

The light-transmitting material consists of an outdoor-facing curved surface, a lower internal-reflection surface, and an indoor-facing curved surface. Together, these surfaces refract, reflect, and diffuse incoming light in the desired direction. The material may be installed at an incline to suit specific building or lighting conditions. Multiple units may also be arranged vertically and horizontally to cover larger openings or provide more uniform daylight distribution.
outputs.L4:
The daylighting structure is designed to introduce natural light efficiently into a building even when the sun is at a low elevation, such as during winter or near sunset. It includes a light-transmitting member installed horizontally or at an oblique angle in a window, skylight, façade opening, or similar building component. The member has one or more curved refracting surfaces that receive incident sunlight and alter its direction. A lower surface is configured to promote internal reflection, causing light that would otherwise travel downward or create glare near the opening to be redirected upward toward the ceiling or farther into the interior.

Through the combined action of refraction and internal reflection, low-angle sunlight is dispersed and guided into useful indoor regions. Even when sunlight enters at an elevation angle of approximately 20 degrees, the structure can reduce concentrated brightness and distribute the light diffusely across the ceiling and into deeper parts of a room. This helps suppress glare and excessive heat or brightness associated with strong setting or winter sunlight while producing more uniform indoor illumination. Because the curved optical surfaces accommodate a range of incident directions, the daylighting effect remains effective despite changes in solar elevation and incoming angle, thereby improving natural lighting throughout the day and across different seasons.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a patent-style abstract describing a daylighting structure that redirects low-elevation sunlight toward a building’s ceiling using refraction, internal reflection, and curved surfaces.
counterfactuals.output: A daylighting structure is configured to redirect low-elevation incident sunlight toward a ceiling of an interior building space. The structure includes a light-transmissive body having an incident surface, one or more curved refractive surfaces, an internal reflective surface, and an output surface. Sunlight entering the incident surface is refracted toward the internal reflective surface, redirected by total internal reflection or a reflective coating, and further refracted by the curved surfaces to form an upwardly directed output beam. The curved surfaces may vary in radius, inclination, or optical power along the structure to accommodate seasonal and diurnal changes in solar elevation while reducing glare and direct transmission into an occupied zone. The output surface distributes the redirected light across the ceiling, from which the light is diffusely reflected into the interior space. The structure may be incorporated into a window, façade panel, clerestory, or glazing assembly and may be formed as a unitary optical element or as an array of elongated optical elements.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe the operation and components of an architectural daylighting device designed to attenuate setting sun and winter sunlight while directing illumination toward the ceiling.
counterfactuals.output:
The device is a **daylight-redirecting light shelf or louver system**, usually installed in the upper portion of a window.

### Components
- **Horizontal or angled reflective shelf/blades** that intercept incoming sunlight  
- **Highly reflective upper surfaces**—often white, polished metal, or specular material  
- **Louvers, baffles, or perforated screens** that reduce glare and excessive heat from low-angle setting or winter sun  
- **Mounting frame and angle-adjustment mechanism**, sometimes fixed and sometimes seasonally adjustable  
- **Ceiling surface**, preferably light colored, which acts as a secondary diffuser

### Operation
Low-angle sunlight strikes the shelf or louver faces rather than entering directly at eye level. Part of the radiation is blocked or absorbed, attenuating glare and solar heat gain. The useful portion is reflected upward onto the ceiling, where it spreads deeper into the room as soft, indirect illumination. The geometry of the blades or shelf is selected to control shallow winter and evening sun angles while preserving diffuse daylight and reducing reliance on electric lighting.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a technical patent summary for a wall-mounted optical daylighting element with an outdoor curved refracting surface, a lower internal-reflection surface, and an indoor curved diffusing surface, including inclined and multi-element installations.
counterfactuals.output:
## Technical Patent Summary

A wall-mounted optical daylighting element is provided for redirecting exterior daylight into an interior space. The element comprises a transparent or translucent optical body configured to extend through, or be mounted within, an opening in a building wall. The optical body includes an outdoor-facing curved refracting surface, a lower light-guiding surface configured to produce internal reflection, and an indoor-facing curved diffusing surface.

Incident daylight entering through the outdoor curved surface is refracted toward the lower light-guiding surface. The curvature and relative orientation of the outdoor surface are selected to receive sunlight and diffuse skylight over a range of solar elevations and azimuths. At least a portion of the refracted light encounters the lower surface at an angle sufficient to produce total internal reflection, thereby redirecting the light inwardly and, in selected embodiments, upwardly toward a ceiling or deeper into the occupied space. The lower surface may alternatively or additionally include a reflective coating, film, textured region, or discrete reflector to support redirection outside the total-internal-reflection range.

The indoor curved surface receives the redirected light and distributes it into the interior. The indoor surface may be convex, concave, compound-curved, faceted, microstructured, frosted, or otherwise configured to provide controlled diffusion, glare reduction, and a desired angular output distribution. Surface curvature and diffusion characteristics may be selected to spread light across a ceiling, work plane, wall, or other target region while limiting direct views of high-luminance exterior light.

The element may be installed substantially horizontally through a vertical wall or at an inclination relative to horizontal. Inclined installations can improve capture at selected solar elevations, alter the internal-reflection geometry, promote upward interior emission, or facilitate drainage and weather sealing. The exterior and interior surfaces may have different optical axes, radii of curvature, or asymmetric profiles to account for wall orientation, latitude, seasonal solar position, and desired interior illumination.

Multiple optical elements may be installed in vertically or horizontally spaced arrays, stacked assemblies, modular panels, or continuous wall systems. Individual elements within a multi-element installation may have common or differing inclinations, dimensions, surface curvatures, refractive indices, diffusion patterns, or output directions. Such arrangements permit staged collection and distribution of daylight over a larger wall area and can provide different interior beam patterns for different portions of a room.

The optical body may be formed from glass, acrylic, polycarbonate, silicone, transparent ceramic, or another weather-resistant light-transmitting material, and may be solid, hollow, laminated, or assembled from optically coupled sections. Peripheral frames, gaskets, thermal breaks, drainage features, ultraviolet-resistant layers, and low-emissivity or selective coatings may be incorporated for structural attachment, environmental sealing, thermal performance, and durability.

The disclosed configuration provides a passive daylighting device capable of collecting exterior light, redirecting it by refraction and internal reflection, and delivering a broadened, glare-reduced light distribution to an interior space without requiring active tracking or electrical power.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Explain in formal engineering language how a transparent daylighting structure redirects low-angle exterior light through focusing, internal reflection, and diffuse emission into a building interior.
counterfactuals.output:
A transparent daylighting structure redirects low-angle exterior illumination by combining refractive concentration, guided propagation, and controlled scattering:

1. **Optical capture and focusing**  
   Low-elevation solar or sky radiation enters through a transparent aperture incorporating curved, prismatic, or Fresnel-type optical surfaces. Refraction at the air–dielectric interface changes the propagation direction in accordance with Snell’s law. The entrance geometry concentrates or collimates the incident flux and directs it toward the structure’s internal light-guiding region.

2. **Propagation by internal reflection**  
   Once coupled into the transparent guide, the light encounters interfaces between the guide material and a lower-refractive-index medium, typically air. Rays striking these interfaces at angles greater than the critical angle undergo total internal reflection. This mechanism transports the captured optical energy through the structure with relatively low loss while redirecting it toward the building interior. Reflective coatings may supplement total internal reflection where the required incidence-angle condition cannot be maintained.

3. **Extraction and diffuse emission**  
   At the interior-facing section, engineered extraction features—such as microprisms, surface textures, embedded scattering particles, or diffusive films—locally disrupt the internal-reflection condition. A controlled fraction of the guided light is therefore refracted or scattered out of the structure. The diffuser broadens the angular distribution, reduces luminance gradients and glare, and produces spatially uniform daylight over the intended interior area.

The overall system thus converts directional, low-angle exterior light into a redistributed interior luminous flux while limiting direct solar penetration and improving daylight uniformity. Its performance depends on entrance acceptance angle, refractive index, optical geometry, surface quality, extraction density, and material absorption.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
